analysis.one_liner: Taxes private equity fund managers' carried interest as ordinary income instead of capital gains.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate Finance Committee hearing or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended, despite 16 sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Investment fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital firms are paid largely with "carried interest"—a share of the fund's profits. The tax code currently taxes those payouts at the lower long-term capital gains rate (up to 20% plus investment taxes) rather than at ordinary income rates (up to 37%). This bill would reclassify carried interest as ordinary income, subject it to self-employment (Medicare) taxes, and close related workarounds such as receiving a partnership interest in place of a salary. The sponsors estimated this would raise tens of billions of dollars over a decade. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on April 15, 2024, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers broadly, since tens of billions of dollars in additional revenue over a decade would come from a small group of the highest-earning fund managers, easing pressure on deficits or other taxes. Medicare's hospital insurance fund would also receive the new self-employment tax revenue. Workers who do not own fund interests pay nothing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal taxpayers and Medicare's trust fund

how_it_helps.text: The bill reclassifies net capital gain allocated to an investment services partnership interest—carried interest—as ordinary income, taxed at rates up to 37% instead of the 20% top capital gains rate [S2].

It subjects carried interest income to self-employment tax under sections 1402 of the tax code and 211(a) of the Social Security Act, directing that revenue toward programs like Medicare's hospital insurance [S2].

It closes loopholes the current law leaves open: partnership interests transferred in place of salary would be taxed at fair market value, profits from selling the carried interest itself would be ordinary income, and SPAC promoter stakes and similar arrangements would be caught by a new general rule [S2].
It repeals the special three-year holding-period break for carried interest created by section 1061 [S2].
It adds a 40% penalty on underpayments attributable to avoiding the new rules, with narrow reasonable-cause exceptions, to discourage structured avoidance [S2].

analysis.who_pays: A concentrated group of the country's highest earners—private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate fund principals whose compensation is mainly carried interest—would pay substantially higher federal taxes. Some of the added cost would likely be passed to fund investors through changed fee structures.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Critics argue the preference is a deliberate feature, not a loophole: taxing a manager's share of long-term fund gains as capital gains matches the character of the underlying asset, and the current law's special deferral treatment applies only when managers hold their stake with real money at risk for at least three years [S2].

Higher taxes on fund managers would reduce after-tax returns on private equity, venture capital, and real estate investment, which opponents said could mean less capital for startups, housing, and energy projects—an effect concentrated in capital-intensive sectors [S2].

The bill is technically dense, relying heavily on Treasury regulations, and managers would face strong incentives and large savings from re-engineering compensation, so avoidance pressure would be substantial despite the 40% penalty [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit—raising roughly $18 billion over ten years from roughly 20,000 of the highest-earning households, and ending a carve-out with no principled basis in the tax code—is real but modest against a roughly $1.8 trillion annual deficit, and Medicare gets a small trust-fund boost. The costs fall almost entirely on fund managers and their investors, with second-order effects on investment in private markets. The burden on fund investors from changed fee structures is speculative but plausible.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act on April 15, 2024, joined by 15 other Democratic senators and independents (14 D, 1 I) [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; the action history records no further action [S4].
The Finance Committee held no hearing or markup, and the full Senate never voted on the bill [S4].
No companion bill was identified in the House [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate fund managers kept the current carried interest tax preference, and their fund investors avoided possible fee changes. Federal taxpayers forgo the revenue the bill would have raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers and the private equity industry

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 15 Senate cosponsors [S3].

for.name: 15 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Brown, Whitehouse, Warren, Klobuchar, Sanders, Manchin, and others [S3].

for.name: Publicly reported estimates
for.role: Industry and policy observers have repeatedly documented the scale of the carried interest tax benefit, which has made the issue prominent in Democratic tax platforms.
for.what_they_did: Sustained public pressure to close the carried interest loophole, keeping the issue on the Democratic agenda across multiple Congresses.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it died in committee [S4].

against.name: Senate Republican Conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, so it had no plausible path to the 60 votes often needed to advance tax legislation in the Senate.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Financial industry trade associations and fund managers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against carried interest tax increases, which have been proposed and defeated in every recent major tax debate; the industry's opposition is a central reason the preference has survived repeated attempts to repeal it.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sen. Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never brought the bill to a vote [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital fund managers
industries.note: Carried interest is the core of these managers' pay; the bill would tax it as ordinary income plus self-employment tax, raising their federal tax bills substantially. Their interest in keeping the preferential rate runs directly against the public's interest in broader, fairer taxation of high earners [S2].

industries.industry: Real estate investment funds and syndicators
industries.note: Real estate partnerships are a major source of carried interest income; the bill's definition of specified assets expressly includes investment real estate, so real estate fund promoters would face the higher ordinary-income rates too [S2].

industries.industry: Private fund investors (pensions, endowments, wealthy individuals)
industries.note: Investors would not be taxed directly, but they could bear some cost through changed fee structures if managers restructure compensation; gains to them from a smaller deficit are diffuse and long-run [S2].
The bill explicitly extends ordinary-income treatment to promoter stakes in special purpose acquisition companies, closing a related tax-favored structure [S2].
